touches.text: build_inspector
Owns the inspectors and gates (9.4): everything in the code pipeline that checks. The exception is diagnostic_inspector, which is base's (17.1).
It outputs only its findings. It certifies nothing, records no crossing, and posts nothing; the gate consumes its findings.

The inspectors are not assumed correct; they are examined when they refuse. After a gate refuses, an LLM sets the refusing sieve's intention and why beside the ticket's intention and why and asks: is this sieve the best we can do right now? If yes, the ticket changes. If no, the sieve is fixed through its own ticket and proof. Either way the system improves. WHY: a disagreement becomes an update to an intention or its implementation, never a conversation about procedure. The sieves stay deterministic and never weigh a why; the LLM check comes only after a failure, and it is never a lock pick because it has no third outcome. Nothing passes a ticket over a red.

Every sieve carries its own why, and the why names where it came from. Akien designed the inspector tools; CC built each specific sieve from what it read him to mean. So the adjudication in 17.11.6 is against the sieve's own why, done by CC, and never a question to him. The sieves are not perfect and nothing here will be: the whole is always under improvement, and each sieve's why is what lets it be judged. Today build_inspector registers 43 sieves, and the 36 sieves/*.json records carry name, band and dials but no why. The whys live only in docstrings.

The same boundary runs wherever Akien designed a tool or machine and CC filled in its specific contents: the nest and its questions, the inspectors and their sieves, the gates and their checks, the corrosion set, the skill doors and their field lists. Each such component's charter carries a design_boundary naming what Akien designed, what CC designed, and how a red over CC's part is settled. CC's part is CC's to adjudicate against its own why. Akien may be asked whether a part could be better, with the whys laid out, and whatever CC can't sort goes to him. A new component that has this boundary declares it in its charter when it is born.

New or changed code (code-seam): at BUILDME the named proof exists and its PROVES names the ticket, and it may be red, since a new proof is red before its build. At PROVED it is sealed green and hollow-measured.
Test runs are transient (30 days, 4.3.2); seals are records of truth (git).

Commit: the proofs of the component the ticket changed, since RULE 1 bounds a change to its component. Passing them puts the component in service, yellow: proven where it changed, not yet measured against what depends on it. In service needs only the best we can do now: 80% trust.

The plan is <id>-<slug>.json: current, one-line outcomes and constraints. The history is <id>.log.jsonl, append-only. Questions live in the outline (0.6.2). A big decision goes in these files; a small one on the ticket.

RULE 1, ENCAPSULATION: every component talks to every other only through that component's public interface: a device's is the bus plus any client tool it publishes; a machine's or tool's is what its entry declares. Nothing outside a device reaches into its code, skills included. A ticket builds inside its own component, and its proofs measure only that component. WHY: it limits a change to the component that made it.
Physics: the encapsulation_holds sieve in build_inspector, a device-path check. Code in device bar may not import cairn.devices.foo except a tool foo publishes. Inside one device nothing is checked.

Any device or machine may have a bin/ beside its code. That folder IS its list of shortcuts: add a file to add one, delete it to remove one. A shortcut is a script that calls the long form (eg `cairn superclaude` -> `cairn cc superclaude`; `cairn show temp` -> `cairn recovery show temp`), which also saves the walk from searching farther, or does work itself (eg install). Shortcuts live beside what they serve (RULE 1). `cairn foo` whose first word is not a device means `cairn cairn foo`: top-level shortcuts are the cairn device's bin/.

Scripts are Python wherever possible, run by Cairn's own interpreter, so one file works on every platform. Platform-specific ones match their platform: executable or .sh on Linux; .bat, .cmd or .ps1 on Windows.
PURPOSE: Python sieves run over a build; reds a component that fails one (no charter, no proofs, a silent device, ...). A new kind of failure found is a new sieve added.

It is the READY TO MERGE ONTO MAIN step of the pipeline: everything's proved, and merging implies pushing it up. With a branch per ticket (3.3.6), commits on the branch are as often as we like; the inspector is the step at ready to merge. Checking what a change touched belongs here; nothing hangs off the git post-commit hook.
Built with the nest machine (16.2).

Once build_inspector moves into CodeMother, code outside her reaches it over the bus: the 18 crossing calls in transitions.py, the other code sites and the 82 proofs that run a sieve over themselves. No published client tool, no fifth exception: that is what the bus is for.

A rule not yet enforced is made into a ticket now, never left floating as prose. So ticket f5dbfddea8c6 makes the rewrites it proposed at the remaining sites (the press office, PROOF.md). Where a site names a rule whose physics is not built, it names that rule's real ticket id, cast now if none exists; the word "ticket" with no id behind it does not count. - CC

A machine made of sieve tools. Each question is a sieve; sieves can come after others. Bands are phases: preprocess, measure, postprocess. A postprocess sieve stamps a rank rather than a cut, and the shake hands back the survivors in rank order (11.4.6).
Sieves measure, never judge: deterministic Python.
INTENTION:

The launcher walks the words. `cairn cairn foo bar` (the long form) means "tell the cairn device to run foo with argument bar". At each level: is the next word a machine here? Step into it and take the next word. Is it a script in this level's bin/? Run it, pass back the result, done. Neither? It is a bus verb: send it to this level over the bus. So `cairn foo bar baz`: foo is a device; it has a machine bar; bar's bin/ has baz, so baz runs. No bar machine? bar goes to foo over the bus. Each check is one directory lookup, so it is fast. WHY scripts first: scripts are the simple path; the bus is the route to what a device answers itself.
A new shortcut needs no watch. Most instance bins are links to their class bin, so the shortcut is reachable the moment its file lands; the build's proof is the whole guarantee.

WHY: the inspector does all the checks, so there is no need for more checks anywhere else. The inspector's output is consumed by the gate. The gate's output is the certificate. (Akien: the design as meant from the start.)
